project.description: This study developed an electric field-enhanced anaerobic ceramic membrane bioreactor (E-AnCMBR) and evaluated its long-term performance (240 days) under applied voltages of 0, 0.8, 1.6, and 3.2 V for treating high-strength wastewater. The optimal voltage for methanogenesis was identified as 1.6 V, achieving COD, NH4+-N, and TP removal efficiencies of 97.3 +/- 1.0%, 30.8 +/- 2.3%, and 29.5 +/- 2.5%, respectively. At this voltage, the maximum steady-state methane yield reached 0.18 L CH4/g COD with a methane content of 80-85%. Electrochemical micro-buffering maintained a stable pH of 8.2 +/- 0.1 and reduced total volatile fatty acids to 130 mg/L, effectively preventing system acidification. Microbial community analysis revealed that 1.6 V favored a dual-dominant archaeal consortium (Methanosarcina 62.9%, Methanosaeta 35.1%) co-enriched with electroactive bacteria, accompanied by higher predicted abundances of genes in acetate cleavage (M00357) and CO2 reduction (M00567) pathways, directly driving enhanced methanogenesis. In contrast, 3.2 V suppressed methanogenesis, shifting the community away from efficient consortia and redirecting metabolic flux toward alternative respiratory pathways. This study demonstrates that moderate voltage regulation optimizes metabolic flux and enhances electron transfer, overcoming mass transfer limitations and providing a mechanistic basis for electro-enhanced anaerobic wastewater treatment.
